title: The more he cut
hook: a Sikh saying of those days: the persecutor was a sickle, the Sikhs a crop that grew back

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mothers in Mannu's prison, remembered in the Ardas. Your line was the mothers kept faith. Who did you do something kind for? Today, what people said about that same governor. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

Mow a lawn on Saturday, and by the next weekend it's back. Cut a pot of mint down to stubs, and it pushes out new leaves. Gardeners know this about some plants: cutting doesn't finish them. Now carry that into Punjab in the hard years, when the governor at Lahore was hunting Sikhs. Out of those years comes a short saying, passed from mouth to mouth, that turns the whole terrible situation into a picture from the fields. Today: the more he cut.
screen: `MOW IT, AND IT COMES BACK.` → `THE HARD YEARS UNDER MANNU.` → `A SAYING FROM THE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the saying, in plain English, because it's a Punjabi folk verse and loses its rhyme in translation. Mannu is our sickle. We are the crop he cuts. And the more Mannu cuts us, the more we grow. That's it. Let's look at it in pieces. First, the sickle. A sickle is a farm tool. It's curved, it's handheld, and it's used at harvest by people who have cut wheat all their lives. The saying takes a feared governor and turns him into a tool in a field. Not a dragon. Not a demon. A sickle. That alone is a kind of courage, and a kind of humor, the dark humor people find when things are at their worst. Second, the crop. The Sikhs picture themselves as something growing, rooted in the soil of Punjab, not as soldiers or victims. A crop belongs to the land. Third, the turn. The more he cuts, the more we grow. It's the gardener's knowledge from the hook, said in defiance. Cutting doesn't finish what has roots. Sikh tradition says the community did keep coming back through those years; that's the story this path has been following, from the hiding to Sirhind. Fourth, the plant itself. The Punjabi word in the saying, soe, is often glossed as dill, a kitchen-garden herb, not a field of wheat. Some readers hear it simply as a crop. Either way, the picture is of something small and green that comes back when it is cut, like the mint in the hook. We grow back.
screen: `MANNU IS OUR SICKLE.` · `WE ARE THE CROP HE CUTS.` · `THE MORE HE CUTS, THE MORE WE GROW.` · `SOE: A HERB THAT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `WE GROW BACK.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, think of a setback. Something that cut you back recently: a no, a loss, a plan that fell apart, a bad week. Breathe slowly. Picture it as a sickle, just a tool that passed through. Then look for the roots: what's still there after the cut? A friend. A skill. A habit. Your breath, right now. Pick one, and picture one new leaf on it. Just one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
datri, a sickle. From a Sikh saying of the hard years: Mannu is our sickle, we are his crop, and the more he cuts, the more we grow. Today's word.
Your line: we grow back. Today, after one small setback, do one small thing that grows back from it, before the day is over. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: The saying about Mannu's sickle is still repeated in Sikh history talks and Punjabi retellings of the eighteenth century as a picture of the community's resilience.
